newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration opposed to encryption bills.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration opposed to encryption bills.

text.p: The Clinton administration remains opposed to Congressional proposals that would dramatically lift export restrictions on encryption technology, a top official said Wednesday.
"We did not support those bills in 1996 and we will not support them in 1997," Under Secretary of Commerce William Reinsch told Reuters.

Earlier, Rep. Bob Goodlatte, R-Va, said he was likely to resubmit a bill that would remove most export limits on computer and communications products that contain encryption -- which scrambles information and renders it unreadable without a password or software key.

Under an executive order signed by President Bill Clinton on Nov. 15, U.S. companies would be allowed to export products containing strong encryption only if the government was able to unscramble coded messages by recovering the keys.

Reinsch heads the adminstration's effort to craft rules and regulations fleshing out the executive order. A draft of the rules was circulated to industry participants this month, but is still being revised, Reinsch said.
Goodlatte blasted the administration's approach, saying it would infringe on privacy rights and hurt software companies.
"I'm sorry that once again an important player has seen fit to draw conclusions before we finished our work," Reinsch said.
Reinsch said that he planned to make changes, after hearing criticisms of the draft rules at a meeting last week. "We will make some changes," he said.
Goodlatte has not submitted comments or recommendations to the Commerce Department, Reinsch said.
